newsitem.title: USA: Lebed aims to create business-oriented party.
newsitem.headline: Lebed aims to create business-oriented party.

text.p: Alexander Lebed, the Russian general ousted as national security adviser and now aiming to become the country's next president, said on Friday his immediate aim was to create a business-oriented political party.
Winding up an American tour clearly aimed at boosting his image in preparation for a future presidential run, Lebed said he saw the United States as a "long-term strategic partner."
"It's clear to me that I will engage in party-building," Lebed told the U.S.-Russia Business Council.

"I need to meet again with professionals in party construction, to listen to analysts and experts, to determine definitively the distribution of political forces in Russia, and to begin serious party-building," he said.
With no party backing, Lebed, who came to prominence through his military exploits in Afghanistan and Moldova, placed third in presidential elections last June behind eventual winner Boris Yeltsin.

In return for backing Yeltsin in a run-off round in July, he was rewarded with the national security post, but was fired Oct. 17 amid fierce jostling for power in Moscow as Yeltsin awaited heart surgery.

Lebed said he expected funding from former military colleagues turned businessmen who were looking for an end to the crime rampant in Russia since the collapse of the Soviet Union -- a major theme of Lebed's political programme.
Other funds would come from party members, he said, noting that 11 million people had voted for him in the presidential elections.

Lebed said major Russian bankers and businessmen were prepared to back him but were concerned he might scare the West. "I hope that after this trip they will stop portraying me as a unpredictable monster," he said.

"I see in the United States a long-term strategic partner," Lebed said. "We are very much alike. We have a mass of potential joint projects, which will have a bearing on stability in many corners of the world."
Lebed has been well received in the United States, winning audiences with Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott and influential Republican Sen. Richard Lugar of Indiana.

But his reputation as the man who negotiated an end this year to Russia's war in Chechnya has been spotted by charges of anti-Semitism and hostility to religion in general. Lebed said he hoped his trip had laid the allegations to rest.
Lebed said he believed he could give a "99 percent guarantee" that the war in Chechnya would not resume.
The retired general said he was "not going to have a hysterical fit" over NATO's planned expansion to include former Soviet allies, which has long been opposed by Moscow.
But he said the alliance needed to change its name, which was a "by-product of the Cold War," and switch its focus to combatting terorism, drug-trafficking, organised crime and ecological disasters.

Lebed repeated allegations that the Islamic purist group Taleban, which has seized control of much of Afghanistan, posed a threat to the former Soviet republics of Central Asia and was out to capture the city of Bukhara in Uzbekistan.
He said Russia should support the forces of Ahmad Shah Masood, military chief of Afghanistan's ousted government, and the northern Afghan leader, Gen. Abdul Rashid Dostum.
"In the past I fought Shah Masood, and today I say we should help him," Lebed declared.
